topics.title: Continents and oceans
topics.intro: There are seven continents and five oceans. Knowing where they are is the starting point for everything else in geography.
topics.hook: Seven continents and five oceans, and the Pacific alone is bigger than all the land on Earth put together.
topics.teach: Name the seven continents, biggest first if you can.
topics.talk: Ask her which ocean you would cross to fly to New York.

topics.title: Lines on the globe
topics.intro: Imaginary lines help us describe where places are and explain climates: the Equator, the tropics, the polar circles and the Prime Meridian.
topics.hook: Top to bottom: Arctic Circle, Tropic of Cancer, Equator, Tropic of Capricorn, Antarctic Circle.
topics.teach: Explain why it is hot near the Equator.
topics.talk: Ask her which hemisphere Australia is in.

topics.title: The United Kingdom
topics.intro: The UK is made of four countries. Let’s learn them, their capitals, the big rivers and the highest mountains.
topics.hook: UK = GB + NI: Great Britain (England, Scotland, Wales) plus Northern Ireland makes four countries.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between Great Britain and the United Kingdom.
topics.talk: Ask her the capital of Wales and the UK’s longest river.

topics.title: Countries of Europe: west and north
topics.hook: Italy is a boot about to kick a football (Sicily); Scandinavia is Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
topics.teach: Describe where Portugal is compared with Spain.
topics.talk: Ask her which countries border France.

topics.title: Countries of Europe: centre and east
topics.hook: The River Danube strings four capitals together: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
topics.teach: Name three countries that border Germany.
topics.talk: Ask her to find Poland on a map.

topics.title: Capitals of Europe: west and north
topics.hook: Make a picture for each: Bern’s bears, Brussels sprouts, Madrid in the middle of Spain, all roads leading to Rome.
topics.teach: Explain how you remember a tricky capital.
topics.talk: Quiz: what is the capital of Norway?

topics.title: Capitals of Europe: centre and east
topics.hook: A HUNGry PEST lives in Budapest (Hungary); you ROAM Romania, then REST in Bucharest.
topics.teach: Name a capital that is NOT the biggest city in its country.
topics.talk: Quiz: what is the capital of Hungary?

topics.title: Air, water and weather
topics.intro: Before we learn about weather, let’s check some ideas about air and water. Many adults get these wrong!
topics.hook: The water cycle is a loop: up as vapour, cool into cloud, fall as rain, collect, and round again.
topics.teach: Explain the water cycle using the words evaporation and condensation.
topics.talk: Ask her why puddles disappear on a sunny day.

items.explain: Asia is the largest continent, with more than half the world’s people.
items.hook: Asia is the giant: the biggest continent AND the most people.
items.example: China and India, the two countries with the most people, are both in Asia, and so is Mount Everest.

items.explain: Africa is the second largest continent, with 54 countries. The Equator crosses it.
items.hook: 54 countries: Africa is a continent, never “a country”.
items.example: The Sahara stretches across the north, Kilimanjaro rises in Tanzania, and the Nile flows north through Egypt.

items.explain: North America includes Canada, the USA, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean.
items.example: New York, Toronto and Mexico City are all in North America, and so is the huge island of Greenland.

items.explain: South America contains the Amazon rainforest and the Andes mountains.
items.hook: South America hangs below North America like an ice-cream cone, joined on by the thin strip of Panama.
items.example: Brazil and the Amazon rainforest fill much of it; the Andes run all the way down the west coast.

items.explain: Antarctica is the coldest continent and is covered in ice. No country owns it.
items.hook: Ant-arctica means “opposite the Arctic”: it sits at the South Pole, the far end of the Earth.
items.example: Emperor penguins breed there, and British scientists work at the Halley and Rothera research stations.

items.explain: Europe is the second smallest continent. The UK is part of it.
items.example: The UK is in Europe: on a clear day you can see France from the white cliffs of Dover, about 33 km away.

items.explain: Oceania includes Australia, New Zealand and many Pacific islands. Some books call this continent Australia.
items.hook: Ocean-ia: mostly ocean, dotted with islands around Australia.
items.example: Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, New Zealand’s volcanoes and the islands of Fiji and Samoa are all in Oceania.

items.explain: The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean.
items.hook: Pacific means “peaceful”: Magellan named it in 1520 after a calm crossing.
items.example: The Mariana Trench, the deepest place on Earth at about 11 km, is in the Pacific.

items.explain: The Atlantic lies between the Americas and Europe and Africa.
items.hook: A for Atlantic, A for America: it is the ocean we fly over to get to America.
items.example: It washes the UK’s west coast, and the Titanic sank in the North Atlantic in 1912.

items.explain: The Indian Ocean lies between Africa, Asia and Australia.
items.hook: Named after India, which pokes down into it like a triangle.
items.example: The Maldives, Mauritius and Madagascar are islands in the Indian Ocean.

items.explain: The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica.
items.hook: The Southern Ocean is the ring of sea that goes all the way round Antarctica.
items.example: In 1916 Ernest Shackleton crossed it in a small lifeboat after his ship, Endurance, was crushed by ice.

items.explain: The Arctic is the smallest ocean, around the North Pole.
items.hook: Arctic comes from the Greek for “bear”: it lies beneath the stars of the Great Bear.
items.example: Polar bears hunt seals on its sea ice, which shrinks a lot each summer.

items.prompt: How many continents are there?
items.explain: Seven: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Oceania.
items.hook: “Eat An Aspirin After A Nighttime Snack”: Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia (Oceania), Antarctica, North and South America.

items.prompt: Which is the largest ocean?
items.explain: The Pacific is bigger than all the land on Earth put together.
items.hook: P for Pacific, P for plenty of room: it covers about a third of the whole Earth.

items.explain: The Equator (0°) divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
items.choosePrompt: Which line is highlighted in red?
items.hook: The Equator divides the Earth into two EQUAL halves.
items.example: It runs through Ecuador (named after it), the Amazon in Brazil, Kenya and Indonesia.

items.explain: The Tropic of Cancer is about 23.5° north. The Sun is directly overhead here at noon on about 21 June.
items.choosePrompt: Which line is highlighted in red?
items.hook: CaNcer has an N for North; CapriCORN has a corn on its foot, down at the bottom.
items.example: It passes through Mexico, the Sahara, Egypt near Aswan, and India.

items.explain: The Tropic of Capricorn is about 23.5° south. The Sun is directly overhead here at noon on about 21 December.
items.choosePrompt: Which line is highlighted in red?
items.hook: CaNcer has an N for North; CapriCORN has a corn on its foot, down at the bottom.
items.example: It runs through Brazil (right by São Paulo), southern Madagascar and the middle of Australia.

items.explain: North of the Arctic Circle (about 66.5° N) there is at least one day a year when the Sun never sets.
items.choosePrompt: Which line is highlighted in red?
items.hook: Inside the Arctic Circle is the land of the midnight Sun: in midsummer it shines all night.
items.example: It crosses Lapland in northern Norway, Sweden and Finland, as well as Russia, Alaska, Canada and Greenland.

items.explain: The Antarctic Circle is about 66.5° south.
items.choosePrompt: Which line is highlighted in red?
items.hook: Antarctic = anti-Arctic: the same circle, mirrored in the south.
items.example: Almost all of Antarctica lies inside it; around 21 June the Sun does not rise there at all.

items.explain: The Prime Meridian (0° longitude) runs through Greenwich in London.
items.choosePrompt: Which line is highlighted in red?
items.hook: Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) is measured from this line: 0° is where world time begins.
items.example: At the Royal Observatory in Greenwich you can stand with one foot in the eastern and one in the western hemisphere.

items.prompt: The Equator divides the Earth into the Northern and ______ Hemispheres.
items.explain: North and South of the Equator are the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
items.hook: Hemi means “half”: a hemisphere is half a sphere.
items.example: Australia and South Africa are in the Southern Hemisphere, so Christmas there is in summer.

items.prompt: Is the UK in the Northern or Southern Hemisphere?
items.explain: The UK is about 50–60° north of the Equator.
items.hook: We are northerners: our summer is in June, Australia’s is in December.
items.example: London is about 51.5° north, roughly 5,700 km north of the Equator.

items.prompt: Why is it usually hotter near the Equator?

options.text: The Sun’s rays hit the ground more directly
The Equator is much closer to the Sun
options.feedback: The difference in distance is tiny. It is about the angle of the Sun’s rays.

options.text: There are more volcanoes heating the ground

items.explain: Near the Equator the Sun is high in the sky, so its energy is spread over a smaller area.
items.hook: Torch test: shine a torch straight down for a small, bright spot; tilt it and the same light spreads out, weaker.
items.example: The midday Sun is much higher over the UK in June than in December, which is a big reason summer is warmer.

items.prompt: Lines that run east–west around the globe, measuring how far north or south you are, are called lines of…
items.explain: Latitude measures north–south (like rungs on a ladder: “lat-itude is flat”). Longitude measures east–west.
items.hook: “Lat is flat”: latitude lines lie flat like ladder rungs; longitude lines are long, running pole to pole.
items.example: London is about 51.5° N and Edinburgh about 56° N, so Edinburgh is further north.

items.explain: England is the largest UK country by area and population.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?
items.example: England is home to London, Birmingham and Manchester, and to most of the UK’s people.

items.explain: Scotland is in the north of Great Britain.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?
items.example: Scotland has Ben Nevis, Loch Ness and the Highlands, plus nearly 800 islands.

items.explain: Wales is in the west of Great Britain.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?
items.hook: Wales bulges out to the west of England: some say it looks like a pig’s head.
items.example: Road signs in Wales are in Welsh and English: “Araf” means “Slow”.

items.explain: Northern Ireland is on the island of Ireland, and is part of the UK.
items.choosePrompt: Which country of the UK is highlighted?
items.hook: Northern Ireland is the only part of the UK with a land border with another country: Ireland.
items.example: See the Giant’s Causeway on its north coast, and the Belfast shipyard where the Titanic was built.

items.explain: London is the capital of England.

items.prompt: What is the capital of England?
items.explain: London is the capital of England.
items.example: The Houses of Parliament and Big Ben stand beside the Thames in London.

items.explain: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Scotland?
items.explain: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.
items.hook: Edinburgh, not Glasgow: Glasgow is bigger, but Edinburgh has the castle and the Scottish Parliament.
items.example: Edinburgh Castle sits on Castle Rock, the plug of an ancient volcano.

items.explain: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Wales?
items.explain: Cardiff is the capital of Wales.
items.example: The Welsh Parliament (the Senedd) and the Principality Stadium are in Cardiff.

items.explain: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Northern Ireland?
items.explain: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.
items.hook: Belfast is in Northern Ireland (UK); Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland.
items.example: The Titanic was built in Belfast, and the Northern Ireland Assembly meets at Stormont.

items.explain: The Thames flows through London to the North Sea. It is the longest river entirely in England.
items.example: The Thames Barrier at Woolwich closes against high tides and storm surges to stop London flooding.

items.explain: The Severn is the UK’s longest river (about 354 km). It starts in Wales.
items.example: Its huge tides push a wave called the Severn Bore upstream, and people surf it.

items.explain: The Trent flows through the Midlands, past Nottingham.
items.hook: Stoke-on-Trent and Burton upon Trent are named after it.
items.example: It flows through the Midlands past Nottingham, then joins the Ouse to make the Humber estuary.

items.explain: The Tay is Scotland’s longest river.
items.hook: Small name, big river: the Tay carries more water than any other river in the UK.
items.example: Dundee stands on the Firth of Tay, crossed by the long Tay Rail Bridge.

items.explain: Part of the Tweed forms the border between England and Scotland.
items.example: Berwick-upon-Tweed, England’s most northerly town, sits at its mouth.

items.prompt: What is the longest river in the UK?
items.explain: Only just! The Severn (about 354 km, from the Welsh mountains to the Bristol Channel) beats the Thames (about 346 km). The Thames is the longest river entirely in England.
items.hook: S comes before T: the Severn comes first, just ahead of the Thames.
items.example: The Severn flows from Plynlimon in mid-Wales through Shrewsbury, Worcester and Gloucester.

items.explain: Ben Nevis (1345 m), in Scotland, is the highest mountain in the UK.
items.example: It towers over Fort William in the Highlands; walkers climb it in the Three Peaks Challenge.

items.explain: Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon), 1085 m, is the highest mountain in Wales.
items.hook: The Three Peaks, tallest first: Ben Nevis (Scotland), Yr Wyddfa (Wales), Scafell Pike (England).
items.example: The Snowdon Mountain Railway carries visitors almost to the summit.

items.explain: Scafell Pike (978 m) in the Lake District is the highest mountain in England.
items.hook: Scafell Pike is the shortest of the Three Peaks, but the top of England.
items.example: It rises above Wasdale in the Lake District, beside Wastwater, England’s deepest lake.

items.prompt: What is the highest mountain in the UK?
items.explain: Ben Nevis in the Scottish Highlands is 1345 m high.
items.hook: Big Ben is a London bell; Ben Nevis is the BIG Ben of mountains.

items.prompt: What is the difference between Great Britain and the United Kingdom?

options.text: The UK also includes Northern Ireland
They are exactly the same thing
options.feedback: Great Britain is an island. The UK is a country that also includes Northern Ireland.

options.text: Great Britain includes Ireland; the UK does not
options.feedback: The Republic of Ireland is a separate country, not part of either.

items.explain: The UK = England + Scotland + Wales + Northern Ireland. Great Britain is the largest island: England, Scotland and Wales.
items.hook: GB = 3 countries on one island. UK = GB + Northern Ireland = 4.
items.example: The UK’s full name is “the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland”: it says so on a British passport.

items.explain: This is the United Kingdom.

items.prompt: What is the capital of the United Kingdom?
items.explain: The capital of the United Kingdom is London.
items.learn: The capital of **the United Kingdom** is **London**.

items.explain: This is Ireland.
items.hook: Ireland is the island to the west of Great Britain; the Republic covers most of it.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Ireland?
items.explain: The capital of Ireland is Dublin.
items.hook: Dublin is in the Republic of Ireland; Belfast is in Northern Ireland, part of the UK.

items.explain: This is France.

items.prompt: What is the capital of France?
items.explain: The capital of France is Paris.
This is Spain.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Spain?
items.explain: The capital of Spain is Madrid. Madrid, not Barcelona.
items.learn: The capital of **Spain** is **Madrid**. Madrid, not Barcelona.
items.hook: M for Madrid, M for Middle: it is right in the middle of Spain.

items.explain: This is Portugal.
items.hook: Portugal is the strip down Spain’s Atlantic side, at the far south-west corner of Europe.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Portugal?
items.explain: The capital of Portugal is Lisbon.
items.hook: Porto gave Portugal its name, but Lisbon is the capital.

items.explain: This is Germany.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Germany?
items.explain: The capital of Germany is Berlin. Berlin, not Munich.
items.learn: The capital of **Germany** is **Berlin**. Berlin, not Munich.
items.example: The Berlin Wall split the city from 1961 to 1989; Berlin became the capital of a reunited Germany in 1990.

items.explain: This is Italy.
items.hook: Italy is shaped like a boot, about to kick a football (Sicily).

items.prompt: What is the capital of Italy?
items.explain: The capital of Italy is Rome. Rome, not Milan.
items.learn: The capital of **Italy** is **Rome**. Rome, not Milan.
items.hook: “All roads lead to Rome”: the Romans built their roads out from their capital.

items.explain: This is the Netherlands.
items.hook: Nether-lands means “low lands”: about a quarter of it lies below sea level.

items.prompt: What is the capital of the Netherlands?
items.explain: The capital of the Netherlands is Amsterdam. Amsterdam is the capital, though the government sits in The Hague.
items.learn: The capital of **the Netherlands** is **Amsterdam**. Amsterdam is the capital, though the government sits in The Hague.

items.explain: This is Belgium.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Belgium?
items.explain: The capital of Belgium is Brussels.
items.hook: Brussels sprouts are named after Brussels, Belgium’s capital.
items.example: Brussels is home to the European Union’s main buildings and NATO’s headquarters.

items.explain: This is Switzerland.
items.hook: Switzerland is landlocked and full of Alps: think cheese, chocolate and mountains.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Switzerland?
items.explain: The capital of Switzerland is Bern. Bern, not Zurich or Geneva, which are bigger.
items.learn: The capital of **Switzerland** is **Bern**. Bern, not Zurich or Geneva, which are bigger.
items.hook: Bern has bears: a bear is on its coat of arms, and real bears live in the city’s Bear Park.

items.explain: This is Austria.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Austria?
items.explain: The capital of Austria is Vienna.
items.example: Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven all lived and worked in Vienna.

items.explain: This is Norway.
items.hook: Norway is long and thin, down Scandinavia’s west coast, with deep fjords.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Norway?
items.explain: The capital of Norway is Oslo.
items.example: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo every December.

items.explain: This is Sweden.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Sweden?
items.explain: The capital of Sweden is Stockholm.
items.example: Stockholm is built on 14 islands, and the other Nobel Prizes are awarded there.

items.explain: This is Finland.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Finland?
items.explain: The capital of Finland is Helsinki.
items.example: Ferries cross from Helsinki to Tallinn, Estonia’s capital, in about two hours.

items.explain: This is Denmark.
items.hook: Denmark is a thumb of land (Jutland) poking north from Germany, plus islands.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Denmark?
items.explain: The capital of Denmark is Copenhagen.
items.example: Copenhagen’s Little Mermaid statue comes from Hans Christian Andersen’s fairy tale.

items.explain: This is Iceland.
items.hook: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so it has volcanoes and hot springs. The word “geyser” comes from Geysir there.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Iceland?
items.explain: The capital of Iceland is Reykjavik.
items.hook: Reykjavik means “smoky bay”, after the steam rising from its hot springs.
items.example: It is the world’s most northerly capital of an independent country.

items.explain: This is Greece.
items.hook: Greece is a hand of peninsulas reaching into the Mediterranean, with thousands of islands.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Greece?
items.explain: The capital of Greece is Athens.
items.hook: Athens is named after the goddess Athena; the Parthenon on the Acropolis was her temple.

items.explain: This is Luxembourg.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Luxembourg?
items.explain: The capital of Luxembourg is Luxembourg. The country and its capital share a name: the city is often called Luxembourg City.
items.learn: The capital of **Luxembourg** is **Luxembourg**. The country and its capital share a name: the city is often called Luxembourg City.

items.explain: This is Poland.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Poland?
items.explain: The capital of Poland is Warsaw.
items.example: Marie Curie, who discovered radium, was born in Warsaw.

items.explain: This is Czechia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Czechia?
items.explain: The capital of Czechia is Prague.
items.hook: “Good King Wenceslas” was a real duke of Bohemia: his statue stands in Prague’s Wenceslas Square.

items.explain: This is Slovakia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Slovakia?
items.explain: The capital of Slovakia is Bratislava. Bratislava: don’t mix it up with Ljubljana (Slovenia).
items.learn: The capital of **Slovakia** is **Bratislava**. Bratislava: don’t mix it up with Ljubljana (Slovenia).
items.hook: Bratislava sits on the Danube right by the Austrian border, only about an hour from Vienna.

items.explain: This is Hungary.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Hungary?
items.explain: The capital of Hungary is Budapest. Budapest: don’t mix it up with Bucharest (Romania).
items.learn: The capital of **Hungary** is **Budapest**. Budapest: don’t mix it up with Bucharest (Romania).
items.hook: A HUNGry PEST: Budapest is Hungary’s. It was two cities, Buda and Pest, either side of the Danube.

items.explain: This is Romania.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Romania?
items.explain: The capital of Romania is Bucharest. Bucharest: don’t mix it up with Budapest (Hungary).
items.learn: The capital of **Romania** is **Bucharest**. Bucharest: don’t mix it up with Budapest (Hungary).
items.hook: ROAM-ania, then REST: you roam Romania, then rest in BuchaREST.

items.explain: This is Bulgaria.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Bulgaria?
items.explain: The capital of Bulgaria is Sofia.
This is Croatia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Croatia?
items.explain: The capital of Croatia is Zagreb.
This is Slovenia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Slovenia?
items.explain: The capital of Slovenia is Ljubljana. Ljubljana: don’t mix it up with Bratislava (Slovakia).
items.learn: The capital of **Slovenia** is **Ljubljana**. Ljubljana: don’t mix it up with Bratislava (Slovakia).
items.hook: sLOVEnia has LOVE hidden in it, and Ljubljana’s symbol is a dragon, on its Dragon Bridge.

items.explain: This is Serbia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Serbia?
items.explain: The capital of Serbia is Belgrade.
items.hook: Belgrade means “white city”. It stands where the River Sava meets the Danube.

items.explain: This is Bosnia and Herzegovina.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina?
items.explain: The capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina is Sarajevo.
items.learn: The capital of **Bosnia and Herzegovina** is **Sarajevo**.
items.example: In Sarajevo in 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand was shot, which set off the First World War.

items.explain: This is Montenegro.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Montenegro?
items.explain: The capital of Montenegro is Podgorica.
This is Albania.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Albania?
items.explain: The capital of Albania is Tirana.
This is North Macedonia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of North Macedonia?
items.explain: The capital of North Macedonia is Skopje.
items.example: Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in 1910.

items.explain: This is Ukraine.
items.hook: Ukraine is the largest country entirely in Europe.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Ukraine?
items.explain: The capital of Ukraine is Kyiv. Kyiv (sometimes spelt Kiev).
items.learn: The capital of **Ukraine** is **Kyiv**. Kyiv (sometimes spelt Kiev).

items.explain: This is Belarus.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Belarus?
items.explain: The capital of Belarus is Minsk.
This is Moldova.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Moldova?
items.explain: The capital of Moldova is Chișinău. Chișinău (you can type Chisinau).
items.learn: The capital of **Moldova** is **Chișinău**. Chișinău (you can type Chisinau).

items.explain: This is Lithuania.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Lithuania?
items.explain: The capital of Lithuania is Vilnius.
items.hook: The Baltic states go alphabetically from north to south: Estonia (Tallinn), Latvia (Riga), Lithuania (Vilnius).

items.explain: This is Latvia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Latvia?
items.explain: The capital of Latvia is Riga.
items.hook: The Baltic states go alphabetically from north to south: Estonia (Tallinn), Latvia (Riga), Lithuania (Vilnius).

items.explain: This is Estonia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Estonia?
items.explain: The capital of Estonia is Tallinn.
items.hook: The Baltic states go alphabetically from north to south: Estonia (Tallinn), Latvia (Riga), Lithuania (Vilnius).

items.explain: This is Russia.
items.hook: Russia is the largest country in the world, stretching from Europe right across Asia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Russia?
items.explain: The capital of Russia is Moscow.
items.hook: Moscow, not St Petersburg: St Petersburg was the capital only from 1712 to 1918.
items.example: Red Square, the Kremlin and the onion domes of St Basil’s Cathedral are in Moscow.

items.explain: This is Malta.
items.hook: Malta is a tiny group of islands just south of Sicily.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Malta?
items.explain: The capital of Malta is Valletta.
This is Cyprus.
items.hook: Cyprus is an island at the far east of the Mediterranean, south of Turkey.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Cyprus?
items.explain: The capital of Cyprus is Nicosia.

items.prompt: Does air have mass (does it weigh anything)?

options.feedback: A common idea, but air is made of particles, and particles have mass. A room’s air can weigh more than you!

options.text: Only when it is cold and wet
options.feedback: Air always has mass, whether it is moving or not.

items.explain: Air is matter: it has mass and takes up space. The weight of air above us causes air pressure.
items.hook: Air is stuff: a football weighs a little more once it is pumped up.
items.example: Crisp packets puff up on a plane because there is less air pressing on them in the cabin.

items.prompt: Is damp (humid) air heavier or lighter than dry air at the same temperature?

options.feedback: Surprising but true: water vapour molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen they replace, so humid air is less dense.
There is a small difference: humid air is slightly lighter.

items.explain: Water vapour (H₂O) has lighter molecules than nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂), so humid air is less dense. That helps it rise and form clouds.
items.hook: H₂O (18) is lighter than N₂ (28) and O₂ (32): swap water vapour in and the air gets lighter.
items.example: Warm, muggy air rises easily, building the towering clouds of a summer thunderstorm.

items.prompt: Why does the Sun appear to move across the sky during the day?

options.text: Because the Earth spins on its axis
Because the Sun travels around the Earth each day
options.feedback: This is what people believed for thousands of years, but it is the Earth that turns.
Clouds are much closer than the Sun and don’t affect where it appears.

items.explain: The Earth rotates once every 24 hours, so the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
items.hook: The Earth turns towards the east, so the Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
items.example: At the Equator the ground spins at about 1,670 km/h, yet we never feel it.

items.prompt: What is it called when liquid water turns into water vapour?
items.explain: Evaporation: the Sun heats water and it turns into vapour.
items.hook: e-VAPOUR-ation: the water escapes as vapour.
items.example: Washing dries on the line and puddles vanish on a sunny day.

items.prompt: What is it called when water vapour cools and turns back into liquid droplets?
items.explain: Condensation forms clouds, and the droplets on a cold window.
items.hook: Condensation: when vapour cools, it comes together into droplets.
items.example: Breathe on a cold mirror, or take a can out of the fridge: droplets appear on the cold surface.

items.prompt: What is the word for water falling from clouds as rain, sleet, snow or hail?
items.explain: Precipitation is any water falling from the sky.
items.example: Rain gauges measure precipitation in millimetres: London gets about 600 mm a year.

items.prompt: What is it called when plants lose water vapour through their leaves?
items.explain: Transpiration: water moves up through a plant and escapes from its leaves.
items.hook: TRANSpiration: plants TRANSfer water out through their leaves, like plant sweat.
items.example: Tie a clear plastic bag over a leafy branch on a sunny day: droplets collect inside within hours.

items.prompt: What is the difference between weather and climate?
items.answer: weather is daily; climate is the average
distractors: they mean exactly the same thing
climate is daily; weather is the average
weather is about rain; climate is about heat
items.explain: Weather is what happens today. Climate is the typical pattern over about 30 years.
items.hook: “Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.”
items.example: The UK’s climate is mild and wet, yet the weather on any one day might be a heatwave or a snowstorm.

items.prompt: Put the water cycle in order, starting with water in the sea.
items.explain: The Sun evaporates water; vapour condenses into clouds; water falls as precipitation; it collects in rivers, lakes and seas.
items.hook: “Every Cloud Pours Constantly”: Evaporation, Condensation, Precipitation, Collection.
items.example: Rain that falls on the Welsh mountains runs down the Severn and back to the sea, ready to evaporate again.
